questions.q: A matmul raises 'mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x10 and 20x5)'. What does this tell you?
options: The GPU ran out of memory
The two tensors' inner dimensions (10 and 20) don't match, which matrix multiplication requires; the fix is upstream, in how one of the tensors was built
The tensors are on different devices
The batch size is too large for the model
questions.explain: Matrix multiplication (m, n) @ (n, p) requires the shared inner dimension to match. Here 10 != 20, so PyTorch refuses the operation and reports exactly which shapes it tried to combine.

questions.q: Why is a NaN loss often harder to debug than a shape-mismatch error?
options: NaN losses never occur in practice
PyTorch silently ignores NaN losses
The code doesn't crash immediately at the cause; the stack trace, if any, points to a later symptom rather than the actual source of the divergence
NaN losses only happen on CPU, never GPU
questions.explain: Unlike a shape mismatch, which raises immediately at the offending line, a NaN loss is a symptom that can propagate silently for several steps before something downstream finally errors, obscuring the real cause (e.g. too-high learning rate, log(0), division by zero).

questions.q: What is a practical way to catch a NaN loss as soon as it appears, rather than discovering it much later?
options: Wait for training to finish and check the final loss value
Check with torch.isnan(loss) immediately after computing the loss each step, and raise or log as soon as it's detected
Switch the model to model.eval() mode
Reduce the batch size to 1
questions.explain: Checking torch.isnan(loss) right after it's computed converts a confusing eventual crash into an immediate, localized signal pointing at the exact step where training diverged.

questions.q: Why are print(tensor.shape) and assert statements described as high-value debugging tools in PyTorch?
options: They are required by PyTorch's API to run any model
They are cheap, immediate ways to confirm your assumptions about shapes, dtypes, and devices, catching problems right where they occur instead of letting them propagate deeper
They automatically fix shape mismatches
They replace the need for a loss function
questions.explain: Printing shapes and asserting expectations let you verify what you believe to be true about a tensor at the exact point it matters, surfacing a wrong assumption immediately rather than several layers downstream.

questions.q: According to the pre-flight debugging checklist, what should you check if a model trained with dropout performs oddly at inference time?
options: Whether the learning rate was too low
Whether the model is in the correct mode — model.train() vs. model.eval() — since dropout and batch norm behave differently in each
Whether the dataset was shuffled
Whether num_workers was set correctly
questions.explain: Layers like dropout and batch norm change behavior between training and evaluation mode. Odd inference behavior after training often traces back to forgetting to switch the model into eval mode.
